item.content:encoded:
The Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS) Refugee Leadership Program Fellowship 2026–2027 is offering a unique paid leadership and advocacy opportunity for individuals living in the United States who have personal experience of forced displacement. The program provides fellows with hands-on experience in refugee rights advocacy, professional development, networking opportunities, and the chance to lead a project connected to their interests and lived experiences.

For the 2026–2027 cohort, CGRS expects to select two Refugee Leadership Program Fellows. The fellowship is designed to bring the knowledge, perspectives, and expertise of people who have experienced forced displacement directly into the organization’s work defending the rights of refugees, asylum seekers, and other people seeking safety in the United States.

Selected fellows will participate remotely for seven months, from October 2026 through mid-June 2027, committing approximately 20 hours per month, or around five hours per week. Each fellow will receive a $6,000 stipend, paid in three installments, as well as an additional $500 professional development allowance.

The application deadline is August 30, 2026.

About the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies

The Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS) is based at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco. The organization works to protect and advance the rights of people seeking asylum and safety through legal expertise, litigation, training, policy advocacy, and other forms of engagement.

CGRS supports attorneys who represent asylum seekers by providing legal expertise, training, and resources. It also litigates cases before immigration courts, the Board of Immigration Appeals, and federal courts to protect individual refugees and strengthen the broader asylum system.

Beyond individual cases, CGRS engages in domestic, regional, and international policy and advocacy efforts focused on advancing the rights and protections of people seeking asylum.

The Refugee Leadership Program builds on this work by recognizing that people who have personally experienced forced displacement possess valuable knowledge and perspectives that can strengthen refugee rights advocacy.

What Is the CGRS Refugee Leadership Program?

The Refugee Leadership Program is a leadership and professional development initiative designed to give people with lived experience of forced displacement an opportunity to participate meaningfully in refugee rights advocacy.

Rather than simply offering participants training, the program gives fellows an opportunity to become actively involved in CGRS’s work. Fellows will collaborate with staff, participate in organizational activities, develop and lead projects, and engage in professional development activities.

The program is based on the principle that advocacy for refugees and displaced people is strengthened when individuals with direct experience of displacement are included in the development of that advocacy.

Through the fellowship, CGRS seeks to foster mutual learning between fellows and staff while incorporating fellows’ experiences and perspectives into the organization’s refugee rights work.

Refugee Leadership Program Fellowship 2026–2027 at a Glance

The key details of the fellowship include:

  • Organization: Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS)
  • Location: Remote
  • Geographic scope: Nationwide within the United States
  • Number of fellows: Two
  • Fellowship period: October 2026 to mid-June 2027
  • Duration: Seven months
  • Time commitment: Approximately 20 hours per month, or 5 hours per week
  • Stipend: $6,000 per fellow
  • Stipend payment: Distributed in three installments
  • Professional development funding: $500 per fellow
  • Application deadline: August 30, 2026
  • Primary focus: Refugee rights, advocacy, leadership, professional development, and community engagement

What Will Refugee Leadership Program Fellows Do?

Selected fellows will participate in several areas of CGRS’s work. The fellowship is structured around three major components: organizational engagement, project leadership, and professional development.

1. Organizational Engagement

Fellows will become part of CGRS’s collaborative working environment.

This may involve:

  • Participating in team meetings
  • Contributing to organizational projects
  • Engaging in initiatives connected to their interests
  • Working collaboratively with CGRS staff
  • Sharing perspectives informed by their lived experiences
  • Learning more about refugee rights advocacy and organizational operations

This component allows fellows to understand how a leading national refugee rights organization develops and implements its advocacy work.

It also provides fellows with an opportunity to contribute their own knowledge rather than participating only as observers.

2. Leading an Individual Project

One of the central elements of the fellowship is the opportunity for each fellow to lead a project.

The project will be shaped by the fellow’s own interests, experiences, skills, and perspectives while contributing to CGRS’s overall mission.

Projects can take different forms depending on the fellow’s background and interests.

Possible project areas include:

  • Research
  • Refugee rights advocacy
  • Educational resources
  • Visual storytelling
  • Other storytelling initiatives
  • Community engagement
  • Public education
  • Advocacy projects
  • Other activities aligned with CGRS’s mission

This flexibility makes the fellowship particularly relevant to applicants with different professional and creative backgrounds.

A fellow interested in research, for example, may develop a research-based project, while someone with experience in community organizing could focus on community engagement or advocacy.

The project should ultimately contribute to the broader goal of protecting the rights and dignity of people seeking safety in the United States.

Professional Development Opportunities

The fellowship also includes professional development opportunities designed to help fellows expand their knowledge, skills, and professional networks.

CGRS will work with fellows to coordinate activities based on their interests.

These may include:

  • Networking events
  • Guest speakers
  • Workshops
  • Training sessions
  • Professional learning opportunities
  • Engagement with colleagues and experts in refugee rights advocacy

This professional development component can help fellows strengthen their careers while building connections with people working in refugee rights, immigration, advocacy, law, policy, community engagement, and related fields.

Fellowship Mentorship and Support

The 2026–2027 cohort will be supported by CGRS throughout the fellowship.

The program is coordinated by a CGRS staff member who will provide overall support to the fellows.

In addition, each fellow will be assigned one or more CGRS staff members as peer mentors.

The mentorship structure is intended to provide fellows with guidance as they participate in organizational activities and develop their individual projects.

This can also create opportunities for fellows to learn from professionals working directly in refugee rights advocacy while contributing their own lived experience and expertise.

How Much Does the Fellowship Pay?

The CGRS Refugee Leadership Program is a paid fellowship.

Each selected fellow will receive a total $6,000 stipend.

The stipend will be distributed in three installments during the fellowship period.

In addition to the stipend, each fellow will receive an additional $500 allocation for professional development opportunities.

This professional development allocation can support activities that help fellows develop their skills, expand their networks, and advance their professional interests.

Where Is the Fellowship Based?

The fellowship is structured as a remote program.

It is open on a nationwide basis to eligible individuals who are currently living in the United States.

Although fellows will work remotely, they must have some flexibility to participate in meetings scheduled during West Coast business hours.

Approximately six hours of the fellow’s total monthly commitment of 20 hours will involve meetings or activities that require availability during those business hours.

Outside of scheduled meetings, fellows have flexibility regarding when they work on their individual projects.

This structure can make the fellowship suitable for people who need some flexibility in managing their professional, educational, community, or personal responsibilities.

Who Is the Fellowship Looking For?

CGRS is particularly interested in individuals who have personally experienced forced displacement across borders.

The organization recognizes that forced displacement can occur for many different reasons. Relevant experiences may include displacement resulting from:

  • Persecution
  • Torture
  • Armed conflict
  • Climate change
  • Environmental disasters
  • Other circumstances that have forced individuals to leave their home countries or communities

Applicants are encouraged to demonstrate how their lived experiences, knowledge, interests, or professional backgrounds could contribute to refugee rights advocacy.

Preferred Areas of Experience and Interest

While CGRS considers a range of experiences and interests, the organization has indicated a strong preference for candidates who have demonstrated experience with or commitment to at least one of its core focus areas.

These include:

Refugee and Immigrant Rights

Applicants with experience advocating for refugee and immigrant rights may be particularly well suited to the program.

This could include community advocacy, organizing, research, education, legal support, public awareness, or other work focused on improving protections for refugees and immigrants.

Legal Protections for Survivors of Gender-Based Violence

Applicants with experience or interest in protecting survivors of gender-based violence are also encouraged to apply.

This area may be particularly relevant to candidates whose advocacy, research, community work, or lived experiences connect with the rights and protection of survivors.

Climate-Induced Displacement

The fellowship also recognizes the growing importance of displacement associated with climate change and environmental disasters.

Applicants with experience or interest in climate-related displacement advocacy may therefore find the fellowship particularly relevant.

Pro Se Support

CGRS also identifies pro se support as an important area.

Pro se support involves efforts to empower and defend asylum seekers who are required to represent themselves in legal proceedings without an attorney.

Applicants who have experience supporting individuals navigating asylum or immigration systems without legal representation may therefore have relevant experience for this fellowship.

Other Related Interests

Applicants do not necessarily need to have experience in one of the specific areas above.

CGRS will also consider candidates whose experiences and interests align with its broader mission of defending the human rights of people seeking safety in the United States.

English-Language Requirement

Fellows must be comfortable working in English.

This includes the ability to:

  • Read in English
  • Write in English
  • Speak in English
  • Communicate effectively with CGRS staff and other fellows
  • Participate in meetings and collaborative activities
  • Work on fellowship projects in an English-language professional environment

Strong English communication skills are therefore important because fellows will participate in organizational meetings, collaborative projects, professional development activities, and other fellowship responsibilities.

Time Commitment and Schedule

The fellowship requires approximately 20 hours per month, equivalent to about 5 hours per week.

While the fellowship provides flexibility for project work, fellows must be available to participate in meetings and other activities during West Coast business hours.

Approximately six of the 20 monthly hours are expected to involve meetings or activities scheduled during those hours.

The remaining time can generally be used flexibly by fellows to work on their projects and other responsibilities associated with the fellowship.

Fellowship Duration

The fellowship will run for seven months, beginning in October 2026 and continuing through mid-June 2027.

During this period, fellows will participate in organizational activities, work with mentors and staff, develop their individual projects, and take part in professional development opportunities.

The yearlong or extended engagement model used by CGRS allows fellows to develop their projects over time rather than participating in a short-term training program.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the 2026–2027 CGRS Refugee Leadership Program Fellowship is August 30, 2026.

Applicants are encouraged to submit their application form by the deadline rather than waiting until the final day.

Only applicants who are selected to proceed to the interview stage will be contacted and invited for an interview.

How to Apply for the CGRS Refugee Leadership Program Fellowship

Applicants interested in the opportunity should complete the application form provided by CGRS.

Before submitting an application, candidates should carefully review the eligibility requirements and consider how their lived experience, interests, skills, and advocacy background connect with CGRS’s mission.

A strong application should demonstrate a clear understanding of refugee rights and the issues affecting people seeking safety, while also showing how the applicant’s own experiences and perspectives could contribute to the fellowship.

Applicants should also consider the type of project they could potentially develop during the fellowship and how that project could contribute to CGRS’s work.

For questions regarding the fellowship, applicants can contact http://cgrs.uclawsf.edu/

When contacting CGRS by email, applicants should include “Refugee Leadership Program” in the subject line.

The organization specifically requests that applicants do not make phone calls regarding the application.

What Makes This Fellowship Different?

The Refugee Leadership Program stands out because it is designed around the participation of people with direct experience of forced displacement.

Rather than treating lived experience simply as a background characteristic, the program seeks to incorporate fellows’ knowledge and perspectives into refugee rights advocacy.

The fellowship combines several valuable components:

  1. Paid participation through a $6,000 stipend.
  2. Professional development through workshops, networking, guest speakers, and training.
  3. Project leadership through an opportunity to develop and lead an individual initiative.
  4. Mentorship from CGRS staff members.
  5. Organizational experience through participation in meetings, projects, and initiatives.
  6. Networking with professionals working in refugee rights advocacy.
  7. Flexible remote participation for eligible people living across the United States.
  8. Additional professional development funding of $500.

Equal Opportunity and Inclusive Hiring

CGRS states that it is an Equal Opportunity Employer and is committed to maintaining an inclusive hiring process and workplace culture.

The organization strongly encourages applications from people who are often underrepresented or marginalized, including:

  • People of color
  • Women
  • LGBTQ+ individuals
  • Formerly incarcerated individuals
  • Individuals with disabilities
  • Members of marginalized communities

This commitment reflects the organization’s broader focus on human rights and inclusion.

Reasonable Accommodation for Applicants with Disabilities

Federal law requires employers to provide reasonable accommodation to qualified individuals with disabilities.

Applicants who require an accommodation to participate in the application process are encouraged to contact CGRS.

Examples of possible reasonable accommodations include:

  • Changes to the application process
  • Documents provided in an alternate format
  • Use of a sign language interpreter
  • Specialized equipment
  • Other appropriate adjustments that enable a qualified applicant to participate in the application process

Applicants who need an accommodation should therefore reach out to the organization rather than allowing an accessibility barrier to prevent them from applying.

To learn more click HERE

Why Consider Applying?

The CGRS Refugee Leadership Program offers more than financial support. It provides a structured opportunity for people with lived experience of forced displacement to participate in meaningful refugee rights advocacy while developing their professional skills and networks.

For individuals interested in refugee and immigrant rights, gender-based violence protections, climate-induced displacement, pro se asylum support, community engagement, research, storytelling, or related human rights issues, the program can provide a valuable platform for turning personal experience and professional interests into practical advocacy.

The opportunity to lead an individual project is particularly significant because fellows can contribute directly to CGRS’s mission while developing a body of work that reflects their own interests and perspectives.

The combination of mentorship, networking, professional development, organizational engagement, and financial compensation makes this a notable opportunity for eligible candidates seeking to strengthen their leadership and advocacy experience.

Click HERE to apply

Key Details to Remember

Before applying, prospective candidates should make sure they understand the main requirements and commitments:

  • The program is for individuals with personal experience of forced displacement across borders.
  • Applicants must currently live in the United States.
  • Applicants must be authorized to work in the United States.
  • Applicants should be comfortable reading, writing, and speaking English.
  • Fellows must commit approximately 20 hours per month.
  • Fellows need flexibility to attend some meetings during West Coast business hours.
  • The fellowship lasts seven months, from October 2026 to mid-June 2027.
  • Two fellows are expected to be selected.
  • Each fellow receives a $6,000 stipend.
  • Each fellow receives an additional $500 for professional development.
  • Fellows will participate in organizational activities and lead an individual project.
  • Professional development includes networking, guest speakers, workshops, and training.
  • The application deadline is August 30, 2026.
  • Only applicants selected for interviews will be contacted.
  • Questions should be directed to http://cgrshires at uclawsf.edu.  with “Refugee Leadership Program” in the subject line.
  • Applicants should not make phone calls regarding the application.

Conclusion

The CGRS Refugee Leadership Program Fellowship 2026–2027 provides a distinctive opportunity for individuals with lived experience of forced displacement to take an active role in refugee rights advocacy in the United States.

With a $6,000 stipend, an additional $500 professional development allocation, mentorship, networking, training, organizational engagement, and the opportunity to lead an individual project, the fellowship combines financial support with meaningful leadership and career development.

The program is particularly relevant to people who want to use their lived experiences and professional interests to contribute to issues such as refugee and immigrant rights, gender-based violence protections, climate-induced displacement, pro se asylum support, and other efforts to protect the human rights of people seeking safety.

Because the fellowship is limited to individuals currently living in the United States who are authorized to work there, prospective applicants should confirm that they satisfy these requirements before applying. Eligible candidates should also consider how their personal experiences, skills, interests, and potential project ideas align with CGRS’s mission.

The application deadline is August 30, 2026, making it important for interested candidates to begin preparing and submit their applications before the closing date.

item.content:encoded:
The American Council of Learned Societies (ACLS) Fellowships 2026–27 are now accepting applications from eligible scholars seeking dedicated time and financial support to pursue significant research and writing projects in the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

The fellowship provides up to $60,000 for a 12-month award period, with shorter awards of six to eleven months receiving a prorated stipend. The programme is designed to support scholars at different stages of their postdoctoral careers, including early-career and established researchers.

Applications are open for projects addressing a broad range of historical periods, geographical regions, disciplines and humanistic methodologies.

ACLS Fellowships 2026–27

The ACLS Fellowship programme supports outstanding scholarship that can make an original and significant contribution to knowledge in the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

For the 2026–27 competition cycle, ACLS plans to award at least 60 fellowships, with approximately half expected to support early-career scholars.

The fellowship is intended to provide scholars with dedicated time for full-time research and/or writing. During the fellowship period, fellows are not permitted to undertake teaching, administrative duties or other major activities.

The fellowship is portable, meaning it may be held at an appropriate location that supports the scholar’s research or writing.

Fellowship Award

Successful applicants can receive a maximum award of $60,000.

The funding structure is:

  • 12-month fellowship: $60,000
  • Six-month fellowship: $30,000
  • Fellowships lasting between six and twelve months are calculated at $5,000 per month.
  • The award period must be dedicated to full-time research and/or writing.

The fellowship must begin no earlier than July 1, 2027, and no later than July 1, 2028.

The fellowship must be completed by December 31, 2028.

At least six months of the fellowship must be completed consecutively. Any remaining months may be completed separately, subject to ACLS requirements.

Additional Financial Support

ACLS also provides award supplements of approximately $3,000 to $6,000 for eligible independent scholars, adjunct faculty and faculty with teaching-intensive roles.

These supplements may help cover expenses incurred during the fellowship period, including:

  • Research support
  • Access to manuscript development workshops
  • Attendance at learned-society conferences
  • Health insurance
  • Dependent care

Who Can Apply for the ACLS Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for scholars working in the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

Eligible applicants must generally meet the following requirements:

1. Citizenship or residency requirement

Applicants must fall into one of the following categories:

  • US citizens
  • US permanent residents
  • Indigenous individuals residing in the United States through rights associated with the Jay Treaty of 1794
  • DACA recipients
  • Asylees
  • Refugees
  • Individuals granted Temporary Protected Status in the United States
  • Foreign nationals who have lived in the United States or US territories for the three years immediately preceding the application deadline, provided they do not establish permanent residence outside the United States during the fellowship period

Therefore, this is not an open worldwide fellowship. Being a scholar from Africa, Asia, Europe or another region does not by itself make someone eligible. Applicants must satisfy ACLS’s specific US citizenship or residency requirements.

2. Academic qualification

Applicants must have:

  • A PhD in the humanities or social sciences, conferred before the application deadline; or
  • Equivalent qualifications demonstrated through publications and professional experience, for established scholars who do not hold a PhD.

A PhD in Education may qualify, but a Doctor of Education (EdD) degree does not qualify under the stated requirements.

APPLY HERE.

What Research Areas Are Eligible?

ACLS invites proposals across disciplines within the humanities and interpretive social sciences.

Projects may focus on:

  • History
  • Literature
  • Languages
  • Philosophy
  • Cultural studies
  • Religious studies
  • Art history
  • Musicology
  • Anthropology where appropriate to humanistic inquiry
  • Interpretive social sciences
  • Other humanistic fields

Research may address any time period or world region.

This means a scholar could propose research relating to Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, North America or another part of the world, provided the project falls within the humanities or interpretive social sciences and the applicant meets the eligibility requirements.

What Types of Projects Does ACLS Support?

The ultimate objective of the research should be a substantial scholarly contribution.

Examples of eligible outcomes include:

  • A scholarly monograph
  • Academic journal articles
  • A publicly engaged humanities project
  • A digital research project
  • A critical edition
  • Scholarly research resources
  • Other substantial forms of scholarly work

Projects can be at different stages of development.

ACLS accepts projects at:

  1. Early stages
  2. Middle stages
  3. Later stages of development

The important consideration is that the fellowship should enable the scholar to make meaningful progress toward a significant scholarly outcome.

Additional Fellowships for Scholars Facing Research Constraints

For the 2026–27 competition, ACLS is offering 10 additional fellowships through anonymous funding.

These fellowships are intended for scholars confronting official constraints on their research and writing because of the contested nature of their fields.

Applicants who believe they qualify should explain in their personal statement the barriers to research and access to knowledge created by forces beyond their campus.

These applicants will be evaluated through the regular ACLS Fellowship competition. Awardees will be selected by expert reviewers from the finalist pool and announced alongside the regular fellowship recipients.

What Projects Are Not Eligible?

ACLS does not support several categories of projects through this fellowship.

These include:

  • Fiction, including novels and films
  • Creative writing
  • Autobiographies and memoirs
  • Creative nonfiction
  • Graphic novels
  • Graphic histories
  • Graphic nonfiction
  • Historical fiction
  • Documentary film production
  • Performing arts works such as plays and musical compositions
  • Textbook preparation or revision
  • Projects primarily focused on pedagogy
  • Educational or technical impact assessments
  • Translation without substantial scholarly interpretation and apparatus
  • Dissertation research
  • Research by students currently enrolled in doctoral programmes
  • Books intended for children or young adults
  • Collection inventories
  • Guidebooks
  • How-to books
  • Self-help books
  • Projects outside the humanities or interpretive social sciences
  • Social science research that does not address humanistic questions or use humanistic methodologies
  • Policy studies

Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed project clearly fits ACLS’s definition of humanities or interpretive social science research.

Additional Opportunities Connected to the ACLS Fellowship

Applicants may also have access to other opportunities connected to the ACLS Fellowship programme.

ACLS/New York Public Library Fellowships

ACLS Fellowship applicants can separately apply for the ACLS/New York Public Library Fellowships, which are offered in partnership with The New York Public Library’s Dorothy and Lewis B. Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers.

The ACLS/NYPL fellowships have the same basic eligibility requirements, application form and schedule as the ACLS Fellowship.

However, applicants must also submit a separate application to the New York Public Library.

The separate NYPL application and three recommendation letters are due by:

September 25, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time.

The ACLS/NYPL fellowship provides a $90,000 stipend.

Up to 15 fellows may receive the residential fellowship and access to the NYPL’s research collections and facilities.

Fellows are required to be in residence from September 2027 through the end of May 2028 and participate in relevant centre activities.

ACLS Project Development Grants

ACLS Fellowship finalists may also be considered for ACLS Project Development Grants.

These grants are intended to support promising projects from faculty at teaching-intensive institutions, including:

  • Minority-serving institutions
  • Regional comprehensive institutions
  • Community colleges

Eligible finalists do not need to submit a separate application for the Project Development Grant.

Selected applicants may receive a $5,000 grant to help advance their research projects.

Named ACLS Fellowships

Some applicants selected through the ACLS Fellowship pool may also receive named fellowships.

These do not require separate applications.

Named opportunities include:

  • ACLS Frederic E. Wakeman, Jr. Fellowships in Chinese History
  • ACLS H. and T. King Fellowships in Ancient American Art and Culture
  • ACLS/Marwan M. and Ute Kraidy Centennial Fellowship in the Study of the Arab World and Latin America
  • ACLS Morton N. Cohen and Richard N. Swift Fellowship
  • ACLS Oscar Handlin Fellowships in American History
  • ACLS Pauline Yu Fellowships in Chinese or Comparative Literature
  • ACLS Susan McClary and Robert Walser Fellowships in Music Studies

These named fellowships target specific areas of scholarship.

CHCI Opportunity for ACLS Fellows

Through a partnership with the Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI), ACLS fellows may have the opportunity to spend all or part of their fellowship term in residence at selected CHCI member organisations.

This is an optional enhancement to the ACLS Fellowship.

It does not require a separate application.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2026–27 ACLS Fellowship is:

September 17, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time.

Applications must be submitted through the ACLS online fellowship and grant administration system.

Results are expected to be communicated by email by April 2027.

For applicants pursuing the separate ACLS/NYPL opportunity, the NYPL application deadline is September 25, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time.

Application Requirements

Applicants must submit their applications online and provide the required materials.

1. Application Form

Applicants must complete the official ACLS Fellowship application form.

2. Research Proposal

The proposal must be no more than three pages, single-spaced.

It must use:

  • Arial or Helvetica
  • 11-point font

Footnotes and endnotes are included in the page limit and may use 10-point font.

The proposal should communicate effectively with both specialists and general readers.

For specialists, applicants should explain:

  • The research question or problem
  • The project’s contribution to the discipline
  • The intellectual significance of the research

For readers outside the applicant’s field, the proposal should:

  • Explain unfamiliar terminology
  • Provide sufficient context
  • Explain potential implications for other scholars or the wider public

3. Supporting Non-Text Materials

Applicants may submit up to two additional pages containing supporting non-text material.

Examples may include:

  • Images
  • Musical scores
  • Similar supporting materials

These materials are optional.

Captions should be brief and descriptive. Any interpretation or argument relating to the material must appear in the main proposal rather than on the additional pages.

4. Work Plan

Applicants must submit a work plan of no more than one page.

It may be presented as:

  • Single-spaced text
  • A timeline
  • A chart

The work plan should clearly explain:

  • What work will be undertaken
  • When the work will take place
  • Where the work will take place
  • How the planned activities fit into the overall research project

5. Bibliography

A bibliography of no more than two pages is required.

It should demonstrate the relevant primary and secondary sources that will be used for the proposed research.

The bibliography should be unannotated.

6. Publications List

Applicants must provide a list of their publications.

The publications list may not exceed two pages.

7. Personal Statement

Applicants must submit a personal statement of up to one page.

The statement should describe:

  • The applicant’s intellectual trajectory
  • Their development as a scholar
  • How the proposed project connects with their personal experience
  • Broader research interests
  • Their motivation for pursuing the research topic or methodology
  • How teaching or classroom experience may influence their research approach, where relevant

Important Application Restrictions

For the 2026–27 competition, ACLS states that:

  • Writing samples will not be accepted.
  • Reference letters will not be accepted.

All uploaded documents must follow the specified formatting requirements.

Documents should have one-inch margins on all sides.

Applicants may use any standard citation style, but citations count toward the relevant page limits.

Applications that do not comply with the required formatting guidelines may be excluded from review.

ACLS also recommends that applicants have an ORCID ID.

How Applications Are Evaluated

ACLS uses a rigorous peer-review process to identify outstanding scholarship.

Reviewers assess applications based on four main criteria.

For more information on ACLS Fellowships 2026–27  VISIT HERE.

1. Contribution to Scholarship

Reviewers consider whether the proposed project could advance its field or fields and make an original and significant contribution to scholarship.

2. Quality of the Proposal

The proposal is assessed for:

  • Clarity
  • Methodology
  • Scope
  • Theoretical framework
  • Engagement with relevant scholarly literature

3. Feasibility

Reviewers consider whether the proposed work can realistically be completed during the fellowship period.

The applicant should demonstrate a clear and achievable plan.

4. Scholarly Record and Career Trajectory

Reviewers consider the applicant’s scholarly achievements and career development.

They also take into account the resources and constraints affecting an applicant’s research career where appropriate.

For the additional fellowships, reviewers may also consider official barriers affecting research and writing because of the contested nature of a scholar’s field.

Commitment to Inclusive Scholarship

ACLS states that it welcomes applications from eligible scholars regardless of:

  • Race
  • Ethnicity
  • National origin
  • Disability
  • Age
  • Other aspects of identity

The programme seeks to support a broad representation of humanistic scholarship and encourages applications from scholars across different types of academic institutions and backgrounds.

However, eligibility is still determined by the programme’s citizenship and residency requirements.

Rules on Other Fellowships and Grants

An ACLS Fellowship may be held concurrently with certain other fellowships, grants and institutional support, including sabbatical support, subject to ACLS’s rules.

For scholars with tenure-track or tenured positions, the combined fellowship stipend and sabbatical salary cannot exceed the scholar’s full academic-year salary.

For scholars without tenure-track academic contracts, combined sources of income cannot exceed 150% of the ACLS award, subject to the programme’s rules.

Applicants should carefully review the official FAQ if they are receiving or expecting other sources of funding.

Resubmissions and Multiple Applications

Applicants may revise and resubmit a previously rejected application if they meet the requirements of the current competition.

Applicants may also apply to multiple ACLS fellowship and grant programmes where appropriate.

However, only one application per competition and deadline may be submitted.

Applicants cannot accept more than one ACLS or ACLS-joint award during the same competition year.

Collaborative Research Projects

ACLS Fellowships are designed for individual researchers, and awards cannot be divided between multiple scholars.

However, researchers working within a collaborative project may apply for individual support.

Each collaborator seeking funding must:

  • Submit a separate application
  • Independently meet the eligibility requirements
  • Clearly explain their individual contribution
  • Explain how the research responsibilities will be divided
  • Explain the relationship between their work and that of the other collaborators

Each application is evaluated independently.

Artificial Intelligence in Applications

ACLS permits applicants to use AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude when preparing their applications.

However, applicants remain responsible for ensuring that their submissions are:

  • Factually accurate
  • Properly referenced
  • Free from plagiarism
  • An accurate representation of their own work

Applicants are encouraged to disclose where and how AI assistance was used for transparency.

Applicant Support and Resources

ACLS provides resources to help applicants understand the fellowship and prepare competitive applications.

These include an informational webinar covering the fellowship and application process.

ACLS also offers online office hours where applicants can ask questions about the competition and application process.

Applicants can also review guidance on writing proposals for ACLS Fellowship competitions and explore information about previous fellows.

How to Apply

Applicants should prepare all required materials carefully and ensure that their research proposal fits the humanities or interpretive social sciences.

The application process involves:

  1. Confirming eligibility.
  2. Developing a suitable research project.
  3. Preparing the research proposal.
  4. Creating a detailed work plan.
  5. Preparing the bibliography.
  6. Preparing the publications list.
  7. Writing the personal statement.
  8. Checking all formatting and page-limit requirements.
  9. Completing the online application form.
  10. Submitting the application before the deadline.

Applications must be submitted through the official ACLS online fellowship and grant administration system.

Application deadline: September 17, 2026, at 5:00 PM Eastern Time.

Opportunity category: Fellowship

Eligible applicants: Scholars who meet the ACLS citizenship/residency requirements and have a PhD in the humanities or social sciences, or established scholars who can demonstrate equivalent professional and publication experience.

Geographic eligibility: This is not a worldwide fellowship. Applicants must be US citizens, permanent residents, certain protected/resident categories, or eligible foreign nationals who have lived in the United States or US territories for the required three-year period immediately before the deadline.

Race/ethnicity: ACLS welcomes eligible applicants regardless of race, ethnicity, national origin, disability, age or other protected characteristics. Eligibility is based on the programme’s stated academic and residency/citizenship requirements rather than race or ethnicity.

item.content:encoded:
Education Cannot Wait (ECW), through its Acceleration Facility (AF), has launched a new Request for Proposals (RFP) seeking qualified organizations, project developers and technical service providers to design and implement an innovative pilot programme in Ethiopia.

The initiative will explore how school-based clean cooking solutions can generate high-quality carbon credits and unlock new climate finance for education.

With international development assistance declining and the need for sustainable education financing growing, the pilot aims to demonstrate how carbon finance can complement traditional education funding while supporting climate action and healthier learning environments.

About the Opportunity

The proposed two-year pilot will combine clean cooking solutions in schools with carbon finance.

Ethiopia presents a significant opportunity for this initiative. Around 90% of the country’s population still lacks access to clean cooking solutions, while the national school feeding programme is expected to reach approximately 21 million children by 2027.

Schools therefore provide an important platform for deploying clean cooking technologies at scale.

The pilot will examine how these solutions can contribute to stronger education systems while generating measurable climate and social benefits.

What Will the Selected Partner Do?

The selected partner will be responsible for designing and implementing the pilot programme and supporting the development of a model that could eventually be scaled.

Key responsibilities include:

  • Conducting feasibility assessments and designing the pilot.
  • Deploying and implementing clean cooking solutions in selected schools.
  • Establishing a robust Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) framework.
  • Generating high-quality carbon credits under internationally recognized standards.
  • Measuring the climate and education-related benefits of the intervention.
  • Producing evidence and learning from the pilot.
  • Exploring opportunities to scale the initiative and mobilize larger amounts of climate finance for education.

Three-Phase Pilot

The two-year pilot will be implemented in three phases.

Phase 1: Feasibility and Pilot Design

The first phase will assess feasibility and develop the design for the clean cooking and carbon finance pilot.

Phase 2: Pilot Implementation

The selected partner will implement the clean cooking intervention in participating schools.

Phase 3: Carbon Credit Generation and Learning

The programme will focus on generating carbon credits, documenting results and producing lessons that can inform future climate financing for education.

Subject to successful completion of these phases, ECW intends to explore scaling the initiative to additional schools and its potential to mobilize larger-scale climate finance in Ethiopia and beyond.

Why Clean Cooking in Schools?

Schools offer a strategic opportunity for testing clean cooking solutions because they can:

  • Operate at scale.
  • Have measurable and consistent fuel consumption patterns.
  • Enable centralized monitoring and verification.
  • Serve as community demonstration sites.
  • Improve air quality and learning environments.
  • Support more sustainable school feeding systems.
  • Create opportunities for generating high-quality carbon credits.

The initiative therefore connects climate action, education, school feeding and innovative finance within one intervention.

Who Can Apply?

ECW is inviting proposals from qualified:

  • Organizations
  • Project developers
  • Technical service providers

Applicants should carefully review the official Request for Proposal and submission documents to determine whether they meet the required technical, organizational and implementation criteria.

Application Requirements

Applicants are required to submit two PDF documents:

  1. Narrative Proposal
  2. Results Framework

Shortlisted partners will subsequently be asked to submit their proposed approach using additional ECW formats.

Proposal Language: English

Applicants should follow the requirements and templates provided in the official RFP documentation.

Important Deadlines

Queries Deadline: 21 August 2026 at 23:59 CET

Proposal Submission Deadline: 25 September 2026 at 23:59 CET

All proposals must be submitted electronically according to the instructions provided by Education Cannot Wait.

How to Apply

Interested organizations and service providers should download and carefully review the official submission documents before preparing their proposals.

Submit Proposals and Queries: rfp@un-ecw.org

Application Materials:

  • Request for Proposal (RFP)
  • Narrative Proposal Template
  • Results Framework Template

Learn More and Access the Application Package:
Education Cannot Wait – Clean Cooking & Climate Finance RFP

Why This Opportunity Matters

This RFP represents an innovative approach to addressing two interconnected challenges: the need for greater climate action and the growing need for sustainable financing for education.

By testing clean cooking solutions in schools and connecting them with carbon finance, the initiative aims to demonstrate how climate-related financing can help strengthen education systems while delivering environmental and community benefits.

The evidence generated through the pilot could also help inform future approaches to climate finance for education in Ethiopia and other contexts.

Conclusion

The Education Cannot Wait Clean Cooking and Climate Finance RFP 2026 provides qualified organizations, project developers and technical service providers with an opportunity to design and implement an innovative climate-finance pilot in Ethiopia.

The initiative seeks to demonstrate how clean cooking in schools can improve learning environments, support school feeding systems, reduce environmental pressures and generate high-quality carbon credits that can unlock additional financing for education.

Organizations with relevant expertise are encouraged to review the official RFP and prepare their submissions ahead of the 25 September 2026 deadline.

item.content:encoded:
Young Social Innovators (YSI) is inviting applications from young people aged 16–21 in the Gorey area to participate in the Youth Climate Justice Project 2026.

The free youth-led project will run from September to December 2026 and will use visual art, digital storytelling and spoken word to help young people explore climate justice and its impact on their communities.

Participants will have the opportunity to examine local environmental challenges while connecting their experiences to wider global climate justice issues.

About the Youth Climate Justice Project

The Youth Climate Justice Project is designed to give young people a creative platform to explore how climate change is affecting their local environment, communities and future opportunities.

Through a series of interactive workshops, participants will explore topics including:

  • Coastal change
  • Biodiversity loss
  • Rural sustainability
  • Community resilience
  • Climate justice
  • Local environmental challenges
  • Global climate change issues

The project encourages young people to use creativity and storytelling to express their experiences, perspectives and ideas about climate change.

What Will Participants Do?

Participants will take part in weekly creative workshops focused on:

Visual Art

Young people will explore climate justice through creative visual expression. No previous experience in traditional art is required.

Digital Storytelling

Participants will learn how to use digital storytelling to communicate climate-related experiences, ideas and community perspectives.

Spoken Word

The workshops will also provide an opportunity for participants to explore spoken word as a creative way of discussing climate justice and environmental change.

The programme emphasizes creative collaboration, youth leadership and storytelling.

Who Can Apply?

The project is looking for 12 young people aged 16–21 who:

  • Live in or are connected to the Gorey area
  • Have an interest in learning more about climate justice
  • Are interested in participating in weekly creative workshops
  • Are willing to explore environmental and community issues through creative expression

You do not need to be an experienced artist to participate. Creativity can take many forms and is not limited to painting or drawing.

Project Facilitator

The workshops will be facilitated by Joy Redmond, a local multidisciplinary artist and YSI Local Leader who has been working with Young Social Innovators since 2024.

Joy has previously facilitated workshops in the area covering topics including Designing Inclusive Cities and Communities, the Sustainable Development Goals, innovation and social enterprise.

Benefits of Participating

Participants will have the opportunity to:

  • Develop creative and storytelling skills
  • Learn more about climate justice and environmental issues
  • Explore local climate challenges and their global connections
  • Express their ideas through art, digital storytelling and spoken word
  • Work collaboratively with other young people
  • Develop greater awareness of community resilience and sustainability
  • Build confidence in communicating their perspectives
  • Take part in a youth-led climate initiative

Programme Details

Project: Youth Climate Justice Project 2026
Organizer: Young Social Innovators
Location: Gorey, Ireland
Venue: Gorey Youth Needs Group Ltd
Age: 16–21
Number of Participants: 12
Dates: September–December 2026
Start Date: 3 September 2026
Schedule: Thursday afternoons
Cost: Free
Materials: All materials provided at no cost

Funding

The initiative is funded by the Department of Education and Youth through the Youth Climate Justice Fund.

The project is one of ten youth-led climate projects supported nationally in 2026.

How to Apply

Young people interested in participating should complete the short application form before the deadline.

Application Deadline: Monday, 24 August 2026

Application Link:
Apply for the Youth Climate Justice Project

Applicants will be informed of the outcome on Friday, 29 August 2026.

Important Information

The project is specifically designed for young people aged 16–21 with an interest in climate justice and creative collaboration.

Participation is completely free, and all materials required for the workshops will be provided.

Interested applicants should also be prepared to attend the weekly Thursday afternoon workshops from September through December.

Conclusion

The Youth Climate Justice Project 2026 provides young people in Gorey with a unique opportunity to explore climate change and climate justice through creativity, storytelling and collaboration.

With free workshops, materials provided, practical creative activities and a focus on youth-led climate action, the project offers participants a meaningful way to understand environmental challenges and share their perspectives.

If you are aged 16–21 and based in or around Gorey, consider applying before the 24 August 2026 deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The NATO’s Future Seminar 2026 is inviting applications from students, researchers and young professionals interested in the future of European defence, transatlantic security and NATO policy.

Organised by YATA Germany, the seminar will take place from 6–8 November 2026 in Berlin, Germany, bringing together approximately 30 emerging security professionals from NATO and Partnership for Peace (PfP) member countries for three days of intensive dialogue, expert exchange, strategic thinking and collaborative learning.

The 2026 edition will focus on the question of Europe’s contribution to NATO and the balance between transatlantic security guarantees and greater European strategic responsibility.

Against the backdrop of the 2026 NATO Summit and continuing debates about European defence capabilities, burden-sharing, deterrence, Russia’s war against Ukraine and the future of transatlantic relations, the seminar will provide participants with an opportunity to examine some of the most important security questions facing the Alliance.

The application deadline is 6 September 2026 at 23:59 CEST.

About NATO’s Future Seminar 2026

NATO’s Future Seminar is an intensive learning and networking programme designed to engage the next generation of professionals working or studying in security, defence, international relations and related fields.

Each year, YATA Germany brings together around 30 students, researchers and young professionals from NATO and PfP member countries.

The seminar provides an environment where participants can interact with:

  • Policymakers
  • Military practitioners
  • Academics
  • Security experts
  • International representatives
  • Young professionals
  • Researchers
  • Other emerging leaders in transatlantic security

Rather than being a traditional academic conference based exclusively on lectures, the seminar combines expert presentations, panel discussions, interactive workshops and strategic foresight exercises.

Participants are expected to contribute actively to discussions and collaborate with other attendees throughout the programme.

2026 Seminar Theme

The overarching theme of the 2026 seminar is:

“Europe’s Contribution to NATO: Between Transatlantic Security Guarantees and Greater Strategic Responsibility.”

The theme reflects a major question facing NATO and its European members: how can Europe assume greater responsibility for its own security while preserving the transatlantic partnership that remains central to NATO?

The seminar will explore questions such as:

  • How can European countries strengthen their contribution to NATO?
  • What military capabilities are required to improve collective defence?
  • How can European Allies close existing defence capability gaps?
  • How can NATO members improve burden-sharing?
  • What role should Europe play in maintaining credible deterrence?
  • How can European countries strengthen military readiness?
  • How should NATO respond to an increasingly complex security environment?
  • How can European Allies sustain long-term support for Ukraine?
  • How can NATO address hybrid threats?
  • How can Europe become a stronger pillar within the Alliance without weakening the transatlantic relationship?

These questions will provide the foundation for discussions and workshops throughout the seminar.

Why the Seminar Is Particularly Relevant in 2026

The 2026 seminar takes place during a period of significant discussion about the future direction of European and transatlantic security.

European countries are facing increasing pressure to strengthen defence capabilities, improve military readiness and assume greater responsibility for collective security.

At the same time, NATO continues to address:

  • Russia’s war against Ukraine
  • Conventional military threats
  • Hybrid threats
  • Cybersecurity challenges
  • Defence capability gaps
  • Burden-sharing
  • Military interoperability
  • Long-term support for Ukraine
  • The future of transatlantic cooperation

The seminar therefore gives young professionals and researchers an opportunity to examine these issues from multiple perspectives.

Participants will not simply learn about current security challenges. They will also be encouraged to think about future scenarios and possible responses.

What Will Participants Gain?

NATO’s Future Seminar 2026 offers participants several academic, professional and networking benefits.

1. Direct Interaction With Security Experts

Participants will have the opportunity to engage directly with policymakers, military practitioners, academics and other international experts.

This provides exposure to perspectives from people working directly within the security and defence environment.

2. Strategic Foresight Experience

Strategic foresight will be an important element of the seminar.

Participants will use foresight methods to examine potential future security scenarios and consider how Europe and NATO could respond to changing circumstances.

This can help participants develop skills in:

  • Scenario analysis
  • Strategic thinking
  • Risk assessment
  • Long-term planning
  • Policy analysis
  • Future-oriented decision-making

3. Interactive Workshops

Participants will select a preferred workshop during the application process.

The two workshop options address different dimensions of Europe’s evolving role within NATO.

4. Professional Networking

The seminar brings together approximately 30 young participants from NATO and PfP countries.

This creates an opportunity to develop professional relationships with people interested in:

  • Defence policy
  • International security
  • NATO
  • European security
  • Military affairs
  • International relations
  • Strategic studies
  • Foreign policy

The relationships developed during the seminar may become valuable for future academic, professional and policy collaborations.

5. Exposure to Germany’s Security Institutions

Participants will also gain first-hand insights into Germany’s security and defence institutions.

This can provide a useful perspective on Germany’s role in European and transatlantic security.

6. Accommodation

Selected participants will receive accommodation for the duration of the seminar.

This reduces one of the major logistical costs associated with attending an international seminar.

7. Partial Travel Reimbursement

Selected participants may also receive partial reimbursement for travel expenses.

The announced reimbursement limits are:

  • Up to €100 for travel within Germany
  • Up to €200 for international travel

Applicants should note that this is partial reimbursement, rather than full coverage of travel expenses.

Workshop I: Advancing European Defence

The first workshop is titled:

“Advancing European Defence: Closing Capability Gaps and Sharing the Burden.”

This workshop focuses on the practical requirements for building a stronger European contribution to NATO.

The central premise is that stronger European defence requires more than simply increasing defence expenditure.

It also requires:

  • Coordinated capability development
  • Greater defence-industrial cooperation
  • Political commitment
  • Military readiness
  • Improved interoperability
  • Better burden-sharing
  • Long-term strategic planning

Participants will examine how European Allies can strengthen their military capabilities and contribute more effectively to NATO’s collective defence.

Strategic Foresight in Workshop I

Strategic foresight methods will be used to help participants examine possible future scenarios.

Participants may consider questions such as:

  • What could European defence look like in the coming years?
  • Which capability gaps could become most significant?
  • How can European countries improve military interoperability?
  • What role should defence-industrial cooperation play?
  • How can European Allies distribute defence responsibilities more effectively?
  • What political challenges could prevent greater European defence integration?

The workshop is particularly relevant to applicants interested in defence policy, military affairs, European security, NATO strategy and defence-industrial issues.

Workshop II: Beyond the Battlefield

The second workshop is titled:

“Beyond the Battlefield: Deterrence, Strategic Resolve and Europe’s Support for Ukraine.”

This workshop focuses on the changing European security environment following Russia’s war against Ukraine.

The conflict has significantly affected European defence planning and NATO’s approach to deterrence and collective security.

The workshop will explore:

  • European support for Ukraine
  • Deterrence against Russia
  • Hybrid threats
  • European security
  • NATO credibility
  • Strategic resolve
  • Future security scenarios

Strategic Foresight in Workshop II

Participants will use scenario-based discussions and strategic foresight exercises to explore potential future developments.

The workshop will encourage participants to consider possible responses to an increasingly uncertain security environment.

Relevant questions may include:

  • How can European countries sustain support for Ukraine?
  • What does credible deterrence require?
  • How should NATO respond to hybrid threats?
  • How could the European security order evolve?
  • What challenges could affect NATO’s credibility?
  • What strategic choices might European Allies face in the future?

This workshop may be particularly suitable for applicants interested in international security, Russia and European security, Ukraine, deterrence, strategic studies, foreign policy and NATO policy.

Who Can Apply for NATO’s Future Seminar 2026?

The programme has specific eligibility requirements.

Applicants should:

  1. Be students, researchers or young professionals.
  2. Be 35 years old or younger.
  3. Hold citizenship of a NATO member country or Partnership for Peace member country.
  4. Demonstrate a strong interest in transatlantic security and defence policy.
  5. Be willing to actively contribute to discussions throughout the seminar.

Eligible Academic and Professional Backgrounds

The application form specifically provides options including:

  • Bachelor’s student
  • Master’s student
  • PhD candidate / researcher
  • Young professional
  • Military personnel
  • Other

Applicants should select the category that most accurately describes their current status.

Is YATA Germany Membership Required?

No.

Membership in YATA Germany is explicitly not required to apply for the seminar.

The application form does ask applicants whether they are currently YATA members and, where applicable, for their national chapter and position. However, applicants who are not members can still apply.

Age Requirement

Applicants must be up to 35 years old.

This makes the programme particularly relevant to emerging professionals and early-career researchers seeking to build experience in international security and defence policy.

Applicants should ensure that their date of birth satisfies the programme’s age requirement.

The application form specifically requests the applicant’s date of birth.

Citizenship Requirement

Citizenship is a key eligibility condition.

Applicants must hold citizenship in either:

  • A NATO member country, or
  • A Partnership for Peace (PfP) member country.

The application form explicitly states:

“Citizenship (must be NATO or PfP state)”

Applicants should therefore confirm that their country of citizenship qualifies before applying.

This is not an unrestricted international seminar open to applicants from every country in the world.

Countries and Regions Represented

Because eligibility is based on NATO and PfP membership, the eligible applicant pool spans countries across several regions, particularly:

  • Europe
  • North America
  • Partner countries in Europe and Eurasia
  • Other countries participating in NATO’s Partnership for Peace framework

Applicants should rely on the current NATO and PfP membership lists when confirming their eligibility, as membership and partnership arrangements can change.

Does Race or Ethnicity Matter?

The published eligibility criteria do not specify a race, ethnicity or racial background requirement.

Eligibility is instead based primarily on:

  • Age
  • Citizenship
  • Academic or professional status
  • Interest in transatlantic security and defence
  • Willingness to participate actively

Therefore, applicants should not assume that they must belong to a particular racial or ethnic group to qualify.

What Should Applicants Submit?

The application requires several pieces of information and supporting material.

Applicants should be prepared to provide:

  • Email address
  • Full name
  • Citizenship
  • Date of birth
  • Sex
  • Current status
  • Current institution or employer
  • YATA membership status
  • Preferred workshop
  • Cover letter
  • CV

Applicants are also asked whether they require accommodation and partial travel reimbursement.

Cover Letter Requirements

One of the most important application components is the cover letter.

The cover letter must be no more than 500 words.

Applicants are asked to explain:

  1. Their motivation for participating in NATO’s Future Seminar 2026.
  2. How their academic or professional background relates to the seminar topic.
  3. Their preferred workshop.

A strong cover letter should therefore be specific rather than generic.

How to Write a Strong Cover Letter

Applicants should consider structuring their cover letter around three central questions.

Why do you want to attend?

Explain what attracts you to the seminar and why its theme is relevant to your academic or professional interests.

Avoid generic statements such as simply saying that you are “passionate about international relations.”

Instead, explain the specific security, defence or transatlantic issue you want to understand better.

What relevant experience do you have?

Connect your academic studies, research, professional experience, military experience, policy work or other relevant activities to the seminar’s theme.

For example, an applicant could discuss experience involving:

  • NATO studies
  • European defence
  • Security policy
  • International relations
  • Strategic studies
  • Defence economics
  • Military affairs
  • Foreign policy
  • Ukraine
  • European security
  • International organizations

Why did you select your preferred workshop?

Applicants should clearly indicate whether they prefer:

  • Workshop I: Advancing European Defence, or
  • Workshop II: Beyond the Battlefield

The explanation should show a genuine connection between the applicant’s interests and the selected workshop.

CV Requirement

Applicants must upload a CV as part of the application.

The CV should clearly present relevant:

  • Academic qualifications
  • Research experience
  • Professional experience
  • Internships
  • Policy activities
  • Military experience
  • Publications
  • Conferences
  • Leadership activities
  • Security or defence-related work

Applicants should prioritize information relevant to the seminar rather than submitting an unnecessarily long CV.

Accommodation and Travel Support

The seminar provides practical support to selected participants.

Accommodation

Accommodation will be provided for the duration of the seminar.

This is particularly useful for participants traveling to Berlin from other cities or countries.

Travel Reimbursement

Partial travel reimbursement is available up to:

€100 for travel within Germany

and

€200 for international travel.

Applicants should understand that the reimbursement is capped and therefore may not cover the full cost of travel.

The application form asks applicants whether they require partial travel reimbursement.

Seminar Location

NATO’s Future Seminar 2026 will take place in:

Berlin, Germany

The seminar will run from:

6–8 November 2026

The three-day programme is designed to combine policy discussions, expert engagement, workshops, networking and strategic foresight activities.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for NATO’s Future Seminar 2026 is:

6 September 2026 at 23:59 CEST.

Applicants should submit their applications before the specified date and time.

Because the deadline is given in Central European Summer Time (CEST), applicants applying from outside Central Europe should convert the deadline to their local time.

Submitting early is recommended to avoid last-minute problems with:

  • CV uploads
  • Cover letter preparation
  • Internet connectivity
  • Application-form errors
  • File-size issues

How to Apply

Applicants should complete the official Application Form and provide all required information.

The application process involves:

  1. Confirming your eligibility.
  2. Providing your email address.
  3. Entering your full name.
  4. Providing your NATO/PfP citizenship.
  5. Entering your date of birth.
  6. Providing your current status.
  7. Entering your institution or employer.
  8. Indicating YATA membership status.
  9. Selecting your preferred workshop.
  10. Preparing a maximum 500-word cover letter.
  11. Uploading your CV.
  12. Indicating whether accommodation is required.
  13. Indicating whether travel reimbursement is required.
  14. Providing the required consent for personal-data processing.
  15. Submitting the completed form before the deadline.

Application Strategy

Applicants can strengthen their chances by making their application directly relevant to the seminar.

Connect Your Background to the Theme

Do not simply list your qualifications.

Explain how your studies or professional experience have prepared you to contribute to conversations about European defence, NATO, transatlantic security or related subjects.

Choose Your Workshop Carefully

The application specifically asks for a preferred workshop.

Applicants should select the workshop that most closely aligns with their interests and experience.

Demonstrate Active Participation

The programme is designed around dialogue and interaction.

Applicants should show that they can contribute ideas, ask informed questions and engage constructively with other participants.

Research Current Security Debates

A strong applicant should be familiar with the major issues surrounding:

  • NATO
  • European defence
  • Transatlantic relations
  • Russia
  • Ukraine
  • Collective defence
  • Deterrence
  • Defence capabilities
  • Burden-sharing
  • Hybrid threats

This knowledge can help make the motivation statement more specific and persuasive.

APPLY HERE

Why Apply to NATO’s Future Seminar 2026?

For emerging security professionals, the seminar can provide an opportunity to combine learning, networking and practical exposure.

Participants can benefit from:

  • Expert engagement
  • Strategic foresight training
  • Policy discussions
  • Interactive workshops
  • Professional networking
  • Exposure to German security institutions
  • Cross-border collaboration
  • Accommodation support
  • Partial travel reimbursement
  • Interaction with peers from NATO and PfP countries

The seminar may be especially valuable for individuals considering careers in:

  • International security
  • Defence policy
  • Diplomacy
  • International relations
  • Government
  • Military affairs
  • Strategic studies
  • Foreign policy
  • European security
  • NATO-related institutions
  • International organizations
  • Policy research

Conclusion

NATO’s Future Seminar 2026 offers a valuable opportunity for young students, researchers and professionals interested in the future of European defence, NATO, transatlantic relations and international security.

Taking place in Berlin from 6–8 November 2026, the three-day seminar will bring together approximately 30 participants from NATO and Partnership for Peace countries for intensive discussions, expert engagement, interactive workshops, strategic foresight exercises and professional networking.

The 2026 programme is particularly timely because it examines Europe’s growing responsibility for collective defence while considering how this increased responsibility can coexist with the transatlantic partnership at the heart of NATO.

Participants can choose between two major thematic workshops. The first focuses on European defence capabilities, readiness, interoperability and burden-sharing, while the second examines deterrence, strategic resolve, hybrid threats and European support for Ukraine.

Beyond the intellectual programme, selected participants will receive accommodation for the duration of the seminar and partial travel reimbursement of up to €100 for travel within Germany or €200 for international travel.

The opportunity is specifically intended for students, researchers and young professionals aged 35 or below who are citizens of NATO or Partnership for Peace member countries. Applicants must demonstrate a strong interest in transatlantic security and defence policy and be prepared to participate actively throughout the seminar. Membership in YATA Germany is not required.
